subChunks.title: LEAD Capstone: Technical Leadership Portfolio
subChunks.hookHtml: This is the culmination of the LEAD tier. You have studied how Lead Engineers think — across architecture governance, organisational design, stakeholder management, system evolution, and engineering strategy. Now you demonstrate that thinking through a portfolio of three interconnected deliverables that a real Lead Engineer would produce. This is not an exam. It is the work.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What This Capstone Assesses

The LEAD capstone asks you to produce the kind of outputs that distinguish a Lead Engineer from a very senior individual contributor. These outputs require:

  • Systems thinking: seeing how technical decisions affect team structure, business outcomes, and long-term system health — not just the immediate engineering problem
  • Stakeholder translation: communicating the same technical reality to engineers, product managers, and executive leadership with appropriate framing for each audience
  • Governance design: creating structures that enable teams to make good decisions independently, rather than requiring the Lead to be present at every decision
  • Honest trade-off reasoning: acknowledging what is genuinely uncertain, what the real costs of each path are, and what the regret-minimising choice looks like
  • People and organisational awareness: understanding that the right technical solution can fail if the team cannot support it, the organisation won't adopt it, or the people involved aren't grown to deliver it

The Three Deliverables

Each deliverable represents a different facet of Lead-level work. They are independent but complementary — you may use the same fictional organisation across all three if you choose.

Deliverable 1: Engineering Strategy Document
Write a one-to-two page engineering strategy for a technical initiative of your choosing. The initiative should be significant enough to require multi-team coordination and a clear business case. Your strategy must include: the business problem being solved, the current technical state and why it is insufficient, your recommended approach with key trade-offs acknowledged, the team and resource requirements, success metrics and how they will be tracked, and the risk and mitigation plan.

Deliverable 2: Architecture Decision Record + RFC Summary
Choose a significant architectural decision (the same initiative from Deliverable 1, or a standalone one). Write a complete ADR for this decision, including all options considered with their real trade-offs. Then write a 150-word RFC summary — the brief you would post to start the review process with the engineering organisation. The ADR is the conclusion; the RFC summary is the opening of the discussion.

Deliverable 3: Team Structure Proposal
You are staffing a new product area (or restructuring an existing one) with 15–25 engineers. Using Team Topologies principles and Conway's Law deliberately, design the team structure. For each team: name, type, member count, owned domains, and primary interaction modes with other teams. Explain how the team structure applies the Inverse Conway Manoeuvre to produce the desired architecture. Identify the cognitive load risk for each team and how you have mitigated it.

Assessment Criteria

Your capstone will be evaluated against these dimensions:

  • Business alignment: does the strategy connect technical decisions to business outcomes, or does it speak only in technical terms?
  • Trade-off honesty: are the downsides of your recommended approach genuinely acknowledged, or glossed over?
  • Specificity: are your action items, metrics, and team structures specific enough to act on, or aspirational?
  • Audience awareness: is the strategy document written for the right audience? Is the RFC summary concise and compelling for an engineering readership?
  • Conway's Law application: does the team structure deliberately produce the architecture, or is it organised by some other principle (alphabetical, org chart, existing team comfort)?
  • Cognitive load management: are team domain boundaries drawn to keep cognitive load manageable, or do teams own disparate unrelated areas?

storyBeats.text: She had been a Senior Engineer for three years — excellent technical work, trusted by her team, reliable in incidents. The promotion to Lead came with a question she hadn't expected: 'What is your strategy?' Not 'what should we build?' Not 'how should we build it?' But: why does this matter for the business, what is the path through the organisation, who needs to be aligned, what does success look like, and how will we know if we're getting there? The transition from Senior to Lead is the transition from answering that question with code to answering it with a document, a team structure, and a conversation.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Director Cass
storyBeats.text: The Lead Capstone is not a test of knowledge. You have proven knowledge through sixteen topics. This is a test of synthesis — can you take everything you know and produce the kind of artefact that actually changes something? A strategy document that nobody reads, an ADR that gets ignored, a team structure that doesn't survive first contact with reality — those are technical deliverables that fail at the human level. The capstone asks you to get both right.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Director Cass
storyBeats.text: The most common failure in capstone deliverables is vagueness dressed as vision. 'We will improve observability across the platform' is not a strategy. 'By Q3, every service will emit structured logs with correlation IDs, measured by zero manual incident trace-backs after that date, implemented by the platform team enabling four product teams through a shared logging library and Golden Path documentation' — that is a strategy. The difference is specificity. Vagueness feels safe because it can't be wrong. Specificity is the only thing that can be right.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Director Cass
storyBeats.text: When you review your deliverables before submitting, ask three questions. First: could an engineer who has never worked with you pick this up and understand what to do? Second: could the VP of Product read the strategy section and understand why this matters without needing to ask a follow-up question? Third: in 18 months, when this decision is being questioned, will the ADR explain why we made this choice well enough that the questioner understands — even if the context has changed? If the answer to any of those is no, rewrite.

learningObjectives: Synthesise LEAD-tier skills — strategy, governance, team design, trade-off reasoning, stakeholder communication — into coherent, actionable deliverables
Write an engineering strategy document that connects technical decisions to business outcomes with measurable success criteria
Produce an Architecture Decision Record that is honest about trade-offs and specific enough to guide future engineers
Design a team structure using Team Topologies and Conway's Law deliberately, with justified cognitive load management
commonMistakes: Writing strategy as aspiration rather than specifics — 'we will improve X' without a measurable outcome, owner, or timeline
ADRs that present only one real option (with two strawmen) rather than genuinely evaluating alternatives
Team structures designed around org chart convenience rather than domain cohesion and cognitive load
RFC summaries written for engineers but delivered to leadership, or vice versa — wrong audience framing destroys credibility
assessmentCriteria: Engineering strategy connects technical work to a specific business outcome with a measurable success metric
ADR includes at least two alternatives with honest pro/con analysis — not a predetermined conclusion in ADR format
Team structure explicitly applies Conway's Law: the stated desired architecture matches the team communication structure
All three deliverables could be acted on by someone who has never worked with the author — no context required to understand what to do
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a Senior Engineer preparing to step into their first Lead role what will be different about the work. What kinds of outputs will they now be responsible for? What does 'strategy' actually mean in practice — not as a word, but as a document someone could act on? What is the hardest part of the transition from Senior to Lead?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Before completing your capstone, review your three proposed deliverables against these diagnostic questions. For each deliverable, answer honestly:

  1. Strategy document: Read your strategy document aloud. After each paragraph, ask: 'so what does this mean for the business?' If you cannot answer in one sentence, the paragraph may be technically correct but strategically weak. Identify one paragraph in your strategy that needs this treatment and rewrite it.
  2. ADR: Show your ADR to someone who disagrees with your recommended option. Can they find the strongest version of the alternative they prefer represented in the 'alternatives considered' section? If not, what is missing? Write the alternative they would want to see.
  3. Team structure: Draw your team structure and then draw the architecture you want to produce. Do the team boundaries match the architectural boundaries? If not, identify where they diverge and why — and whether that divergence is intentional.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
This guided practice is a self-review exercise — there is no single correct answer. The model approach for each:

1. Strategy document — 'so what?' test:
A technically correct paragraph might read: 'We will migrate authentication from session-based to JWT by adopting the spring-security-oauth2-resource-server library, which supports RS256 token validation and integrates with our existing Spring Security configuration.'
After asking 'so what for the business?': 'This migration reduces our security audit scope by removing four services from PCI DSS compliance requirements, saving an estimated 60 engineer-hours per annual audit and reducing our audit risk exposure.' The technical paragraph is correct; the business paragraph is what makes it a strategy. Both are necessary. The rewrite puts the business outcome first and the technical mechanism second.

2. ADR — alternative that disagrees:
If your ADR recommends event-driven integration and your alternatives section covers only 'do nothing' and 'use a service mesh' — a reviewer who advocates for synchronous API gateway pattern will find their preference missing. A complete alternatives section would include: 'API Gateway with synchronous aggregation — Pro: simpler mental model, strong consistency, easier debugging. Con: gateway becomes a bottleneck, every consumer couples to the gateway's aggregation logic, scaling requires scaling the gateway. Rejected because: at projected traffic of 10,000 req/s, gateway becomes a single point of failure and a deployment bottleneck. Event-driven allows independent scaling.' The alternative is represented fully and rejected with specific reasons — not strawmanned.

3. Team structure vs architecture match:
If the desired architecture is: independent spell service, user service, commerce service, and shared platform — then the team structure should have exactly those four boundaries (plus a platform team). If the team structure groups 'spell and commerce' together because those engineers already sit near each other, the team boundary and the architectural boundary diverge. Conway's Law will then produce a spell+commerce combined service rather than two independent ones. The divergence is either intentional (accepted coupling) or a mistake (team convenience overriding architecture). Name which it is, and if a mistake, correct it.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Complete your LEAD Capstone. Choose a fictional or real organisation — a startup, a scale-up, or a division of a large company. You will produce all three deliverables for this organisation.

Organisation context: The Academy Engineering — 120 engineers, 8 product teams, 35 services. The organisation is 4 years old. The monolith that powered the first 2 years is still running alongside 35 microservices, 12 of which have direct REST integrations into the monolith. The authentication system is homegrown basic auth. The observability posture is inconsistent — 6 services have structured logging; 29 use System.out.println. There is no incident management process. The team structure was drawn along existing friend-group lines rather than domain boundaries.

Deliverable 1 (Engineering Strategy): Choose one of the three problems (monolith integration, authentication modernisation, or observability) and write a full engineering strategy document. Required sections: Problem & Business Impact, Current State Analysis, Recommended Approach, Alternatives Summary, Team & Resource Requirements, Success Metrics, Risks & Mitigations.

Deliverable 2 (ADR + RFC Summary): Write a complete ADR for the key architectural decision within your chosen strategy. Write a 150-word RFC summary to open the review process.

Deliverable 3 (Team Structure): Redesign the 120-engineer, 8-team structure using Team Topologies. Use Conway's Law deliberately. Show how the new structure produces the architecture the strategy requires. Justify each team boundary against cognitive load principles.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A complete capstone at this scale is intentionally too long for a single model answer. The following outlines the expected standard for each deliverable:

DELIVERABLE 1 — Engineering Strategy (Observability example):

Problem & Business Impact:
Must quantify: '29 of 35 services have no structured logging. Average incident MTTR is 4.2 hours because engineers spend the first 2–3 hours reconstructing what happened from printf statements in Cloudwatch.' Business impact: estimated 8 engineer-days/month lost to slow incident diagnosis. Each hour of p1 incident costs approximately £X in lost bookings. This is not a technical problem — it is a business reliability problem.

Recommended Approach:
Not 'add logging' — a specific plan: platform team builds academy-logging-starter (Maven BOM, SLF4J JSON layout, MDC correlation propagation), enabling team embeds with 2 product teams per month for 4 months, and a fitness function (CI check) detects System.out.println usage as a build advisory after month 3.

Success Metrics:
- 90% of services emitting structured JSON logs by end Q3 (measurable via log pipeline sampling)
- Average incident MTTR under 45 minutes (measured from incident log, compared to current 4.2 hours)
- Zero incidents where root cause cannot be traced from logs (measured via post-incident PIR analysis)

ADR format:
Status: Proposed. Context: [describes the observability problem with data]. Decision: adopt SLF4J + Logback JSON layout as the organisation standard for all structured logging. Options Considered: (1) Datadog APM agent — rejected because cost at 35 services is £3,200/month; logging layer is sufficient for current needs. (2) OpenTelemetry — viable future direction but adds complexity before basics are in place; ADR to be revisited in 12 months. (3) SLF4J + structured layout (recommended). Consequences: 35 services must migrate; platform team owns the library; product teams own the migration within their services.

RFC Summary (150 words):
'We are proposing to standardise all Academy services on SLF4J structured JSON logging with a shared academy-logging-starter library. Context: 29 of 35 services currently log with System.out.println. Average incident MTTR is 4.2 hours, largely because reconstructing what happened requires manual correlation of unstructured output. The proposal: platform team ships academy-logging-starter by Feb 1 (3-week build). Enabling team runs 2-week engagements with each product team through Q2; all services migrated by end Q3. A CI advisory (not a blocker) detects new println usage after March 1. Full CI enforcement after September 1. We are not proposing OpenTelemetry or APM tooling at this stage — structured logs are the necessary foundation. Comments by [date+7]; decision by [date+10]. Key open question: should the CI check be advisory or blocking from day 1?'

TEAM STRUCTURE — Conway's Law application:
For an observability-first architecture, the desired system structure is: 6 independent product services + 1 platform service (logging/metrics/tracing). Therefore the team structure should be:
- 6 stream-aligned product teams (15–18 engineers each) — each owns their domain and their service's observability implementation
- 1 platform team (8 engineers) — owns academy-logging-starter, metrics pipeline, alerting standards, Golden Paths
- 1 enabling team (4 engineers, 6-month charter) — embeds with product teams to drive adoption, then disbands or recharges to next initiative

Cognitive load:
- Each stream team: owns 2–3 related services in one domain. Risk: feature volume. Mitigation: platform team handles all cross-cutting concerns (logging, CI, deployment) so stream teams focus on domain logic only.
- Platform team: 8 engineers serving 120 customers. Risk: being stretched too thin. Mitigation: self-service Golden Paths reduce demand; the team measures adoption rather than feature count.
- Enabling team: temporary — 6-month charter, then evaluated. Risk: becoming a permanent support resource. Mitigation: charter is explicit; success criterion is that each product team is self-sufficient by the end of the engagement.

questions.prompt: A Lead's engineering strategy document begins: 'We propose to implement distributed tracing using OpenTelemetry across all 35 services, leveraging the W3C Trace Context propagation standard and integrating with our existing Jaeger backend.' This is the first paragraph. What is wrong with this as the opening of a strategy document?
options: OpenTelemetry is the wrong technology choice

The opening paragraph describes the technical solution before establishing what business problem it solves or why stakeholders should care — it is written in discovery order rather than decision order
A strategy document should not mention specific technologies
The paragraph is too short to be meaningful
questions.answer: The opening paragraph describes the technical solution before establishing what business problem it solves or why stakeholders should care — it is written in discovery order rather than decision order
questions.explanation: A strategy document that opens with the technical solution loses non-technical readers before the first sentence is finished. The opening paragraph of a strategy must answer: what problem are we solving and why does it matter for the business? 'Our engineers spend an average of 3 hours per incident reconstructing what happened across services because we have no distributed tracing. We lose approximately 8 engineer-days per month and £X in reliability costs. This strategy proposes solving that.' — that is the opening. The technical solution (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, W3C propagation) comes later, for the section that addresses how.

questions.prompt: A Lead designs a team structure for a new product area by grouping engineers who already know each other well into teams, reasoning that trust and communication will be high. What architectural risk does this create according to Conway's Law?
options: No risk — team trust is the most important factor in software delivery
The architecture will emerge to mirror the social groupings rather than the desired domain boundaries — producing services with boundaries that reflect friendships rather than business domains
The teams will have too much autonomy and will diverge from the company standards
Performance reviews will be harder to conduct if teams are based on social relationships
questions.answer: The architecture will emerge to mirror the social groupings rather than the desired domain boundaries — producing services with boundaries that reflect friendships rather than business domains
questions.explanation: Conway's Law is not optional — it operates regardless of intent. If teams are organised around social familiarity rather than domain ownership, the communication structure will produce architecture that reflects those social groupings. A team of friends who work on both payment and tournament features will produce a payment+tournament service (or tight coupling between the two), even if the desired architecture keeps them independent. The Inverse Conway Manoeuvre applies deliberately: decide the architecture first, then structure teams to match it. Team trust matters — but it can be built within correctly-bounded teams; it should not be the primary driver of team boundary decisions.

questions.prompt: An Architecture Decision Record that presents three options — the recommended option in full detail, plus two obviously inferior alternatives with minimal analysis — satisfies the 'alternatives considered' requirement of a good ADR.
questions.explanation: An ADR with strawman alternatives does not satisfy the requirement — it satisfies the form while violating the function. The purpose of alternatives considered is to demonstrate that the author genuinely evaluated other paths and chose this one for specific, articulable reasons. Each alternative should be presented at its best: what are its genuine advantages? Why would a reasonable engineer choose it? Only then does explaining why it was not chosen become credible. An ADR where the alternatives are obviously inferior from the first sentence signals that the author reverse-engineered justification for a predetermined conclusion — the opposite of good decision documentation.
